owe.e:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyḱ-
Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂óyḱe
Proto-Germanic *aiganą
Proto-West Germanic *aigan
Old English āgan
Middle English owen
English owe
From Middle English owen, from Old English āgan, from Proto-West Germanic *aigan (“to own”), from Proto-Germanic *aiganą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂óyḱe (“to possess, own”), reduplicated stative of *h₂eyḱ- (“to own”). See also own, ought.
Cognate with Sanskrit ईष्टे (īṣṭe, “to own, possess”).

s.d: be obliged to pay or repay
be indebted to, in an abstract or intellectual sense
x: This new theory owes much to Einstein's Relativity Theory

s.d: be in debt
x: She owes me $200
I still owe for the car

s.d: To be under an obligation to give something back to someone or to perform some action for someone.
x: We owe it to our children to make our nation a better place to live in the future.
I owe Kevin five bucks which he lent to me last week.

s.d: To have as a cause; used with to.
x: The record owes its success to the outstanding guitar solos.

s.d: owed as a debt
x: outstanding bills
undischarged debts

owl.e:
Etymology tree
Proto-Germanic *uwwô
Proto-Germanic *-ulǭ
Proto-Germanic *uwwulǭ
Proto-West Germanic *uwwulā
Old English ūle
Middle English oule
English owl
From Middle English howle, oul, oule, owle, owlle, from Old English ūle, from Proto-West Germanic *uwwulā, from Proto-Germanic *uwwulǭ (“owl”), diminutive of *uwwǭ (“eagle-owl”), of imitative origin or a variant of *ūfaz, *ūfǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *up- (“to cry out”).
Cognates
Cognate with Scots oul (“owl”), Saterland Frisian Ule (“owl”)

s.d: nocturnal bird of prey with hawk-like beak and claws and large head with front-facing eyes

Any of various birds of prey of the order Strigiformes, families Strigidae and Tytonidae, that are primarily nocturnal and have forward-looking, binocular vision, limited eye movement, and good hearing.
x: A group of owls is called a parliament.

s.d: A person seen as having owl-like characteristics, especially appearing wise or serious, or being nocturnally active.
An owl pigeon.
A politician with moderate views that are neither hawkish nor dovish.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies, especially in the genus Caligo, having large eyespots on the wings.
(archaic) To smuggle contraband goods.
stout perennial herb of western United States having flower heads with drooping orange-yellow rays; causes spewing sickness in sheep
young owl
One of a species of small owls, such as Athene noctua.
An owlet moth.
x: Noticeable features found in many of the owlets are two markings that often appear on the upper forewings.

owlet moth.e: Partial calque of translingual Noctua (genus of moths, type genus of the family Noctuidae, literally “owl”) + moth.

s.d: usually dull-colored medium-sized nocturnal moth; the usually smooth-bodied larvae are destructive agricultural pests
Any moth of the family Noctuidae.

owlish.e:
Etymology tree
English owl
Proto-Indo-European *-iskos
Proto-Germanic *-iskaz
Proto-West Germanic *-isk
Old English -isċ
Middle English -isch
English -ish
English owlish
From owl + -ish.

s.d: resembling an owl; solemn and wise in appearance
Resembling or characteristic of an owl.
x:
1914, Theodore Dreiser, The Titan, Chapter 26, http://gutenberg.net.au/ebooks/fr100299.txt
"You're very right," he said, with owlish smugness, adjusting a waistcoat button that had come loose, and smoothing his cuffs.
He feebly wanted to get out of this, away from clucking nurses and Dr. Crittenham's owlish peering and the horrible scrambled eggs and cold toast.

s.d: Wise and solemn.
x: He stands precociously possessed of centuries of owlish wisdom.
[…] their large black eyes scanned the drawings with the owlish look of wisdom peculiar to connoisseurs.

s.d: Stupid; dull-looking.
x: But, indeed, the young Venetian is, at that age when all men are owlish, ignorant, and vapid, the most owlish, ignorant, and vapid man in the world.
"Any more big words coming?" he asked. "Owlish, stupid, brutal, unloving? That's you all over. Have you murdered anybody?"

owlishly.e:
Etymology tree
English owlish
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English owlishly
From owlish + -ly.

s.d: in an owlish manner
x: the gentle-looking barrister peered owlishly around him

s.d: In an owlish manner, especially with regard to looking.
x: To the muzzy drumming of beer in his veins he gazed long and owlishly at the sombre cottage[.]
He gazed owlishly down at his confederates and they gazed owlishly back at him.

own.e:
From Middle English oun, owen, from Old English āgen (“own, proper, peculiar”), originally the past participle of āgan; from Proto-West Germanic *aigan (“own”), from Proto-Germanic *aiganaz (“own”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyḱ- (“to have, possess”). Doublet of eigen-.
Cognates
Cognate with Scots ain, awin, awn, ayn (“own”), Saterland Frisian oain (“own”), West Frisian, Dutch, and German eigen (“own”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Swedish egen (“own”), Faroese egin (“own”), Icelandic eigin,

s.d: A crushing insult.
x: the amount of bigots that just screenshot my profile thinking it's the biggest own is insane.

s.d: have ownership or possession of
x: He owns three houses in Florida
How many cars does she have?

s.d: To have rightful possession of (property, goods or capital); to have legal title to; to acquire a property or asset.
x: I own this car.

s.d: To have recognized political sovereignty over a place, territory, as distinct from the ordinary connotation of property ownership.
x: The United States owns Point Roberts by the terms of the Treaty of Oregon.

s.d: (informal) To defeat or embarrass; to overwhelm.
x: I will own my enemies.
If he wins, he will own you.

s.d: To virtually or figuratively enslave.
(slang) To defeat, dominate, or be above.
(slang) To illicitly obtain administrative access to a computer system, thereby having full access to all the files thereon (including executables).
x: "TH15 5Y5T3M 15 0WN3D"

s.d: (slang) To be very good.
To admit, concede, grant, allow; not to deny.
x: I own thy speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me.

For instance, when I flung the cat out of an upper window (though I did it from no ill-feeling, and it didn't hurt the cat), I was ready, after a moment's reflection, to own I was wrong, as a gentleman should.

s.d: To acknowledge.
x: I must own that I have been at fault all this time.
Two of those fellows you must know and own.

s.d: To proudly acknowledge; to not be ashamed or embarrassed of.
x: "Well, I'm not hiding anymore! I'm owning my girly looks with cute short pink hair!"

s.d: To take responsibility for.
To recognise.
x: I own him as a son of my own.

s.d: belonging to or on behalf of a specified person (especially yourself); preceded by a possessive
x: for your own use
do your own thing

s.d: Belonging to; possessed; acquired and designated by; proper to; property of; titled to; held in one's name; under/using the name of. Often marks a possessive determiner as reflexive, referring back to the subject of the clause or sentence.
x: The fathers shall not bee put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: euery man shall be put to death for his owne sinne.
Prospero: Fairely ſpoke ; / Sit then, and talke with her, ſhe is thine owne ;

s.d: Not shared.
x: When we move into the new house, the kids will each have their own bedroom.

s.d: (obsolete) Peculiar, domestic.
(obsolete) Not foreign.
(soccer) a goal that results when a player inadvertently knocks the ball into the goal they are defending
x: the own goal cost them the game

s.d: A goal that results from a player putting the ball or puck into the goal of their own team; the resulting goal being scored for the opposition.
x: Madagascar's soccer authorities have banned Stade Olympique de L'Emyrne (SOE)'s coach and four of the team's players after they scored a world record 149 own goals in a match last month.
It is 20 years to the day since Escobar was shot dead after scoring the own goal that effectively sealed Colombia’s elimination from USA ’94.

s.d: (figuratively) A blunder that damages one’s own prospects.
x: No doubt the buzz of army helicopters will sound again in the skies over Belfast tonight, as loyalists continue to score this series of bloody own goals.

s.d: admit or acknowledge a wrongdoing or error
x: the writer of the anonymous letter owned up after they identified his handwriting

s.d: having an owner; often used in combination
x: state-owned railways

s.d: Having an owner who is part of a specified group.
x: black-owned; veteran-owned; woman-owned

Since PG&E is an investor-owned utility, this is good news for its shareholders. But not so much for its customers whose costs keep rising and whose electricity is shut off when there are high winds or extreme heat.

owner.e: Inherited from Middle English ouner, from Old English āgnere. By surface analysis, own + -er, though etymologically own is a back-formation from owner.

s.d: (law) someone who owns (is legal possessor of) a business
x: he is the owner of a chain of restaurants

s.d: a person who owns something
x: they are searching for the owner of the car
who is the owner of that friendly smile?

s.d: (slang) The captain of a ship.
the owner's investment in the business which consists of the net assets of an entity.
x: The types of accounts and their description that comprise the owner's equity depend on the nature of the entity and may include: common stock, capital surplus, retained earnings, and reserve.

s.d: (uncountable) Synonym of ownership equity.
a motorist who owns the car that he/she drives
a person who owns the vehicle they drive as a part of their job
a NASCAR driver who fully or partially owns the team they are driving for
lived in by the owner
x: one owner-occupied and three rental apartments

s.d: an occupant who owns the home that he/she lives in
homeowner
having no owner

Etymology tree
Middle English ouner
English owner
Proto-Germanic *skapjaną
Proto-Germanic *-skapiz
Proto-West Germanic *-skapi
Old English -sċiepe
Middle English -schipe

From owner + -ship.

s.d: the relation of an owner to the thing possessed; possession with the right to transfer possession to others
the act of having and controlling property
the state or fact of being an owner
(uncountable) The state of having complete legal control of something; possession; proprietorship.
x: In the summer, DCC [Devon County Council] transferred ownership of the northern part of the station to NR for a nominal £1, enabling it (and the platform) to become part of the rail network.

s.d: (uncountable) Responsibility for or control over something.
x: The successful candidate will take ownership of all internal design projects.
